key_facts: **No comedones?** Think rosacea, perioral dermatitis, steroid acne or folliculitis rather than acne vulgaris.
**Rosacea**: age 30–60, flushing, central face; avoid topical steroids. **Rosacea fulminans**: explosive facial nodules in young women.
**Steroid acne**: sudden monomorphic papules/pustules on chest and back after oral, inhaled, topical or bleaching steroids.
**Gram-negative folliculitis** after long-term tetracyclines: stop the tetracycline, swab, refer.
**Malassezia folliculitis**: itchy uniform papules on upper trunk; **hot-tub folliculitis**: *Pseudomonas*, settles in days.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: This is a **differential page**: conditions that look like acne but need different treatment. Rosacea and perioral dermatitis have their own pages.

Not every facial papule is acne. This page covers the common **mimics** taught with Module 6 Week 2: **rosacea** (and rosacea fulminans), **steroid-induced** acne/rosacea/perioral dermatitis, and **folliculitis variants** (Gram-negative, Malassezia, *Pseudomonas*/hot-tub).
True acne vulgaris is covered separately: [acne vulgaris](condition:acne-vulgaris).

ul: **Rosacea:** neurovascular dysregulation, innate immunity (cathelicidin), *Demodex*, UV; triggers include heat, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, topical steroids.
**Steroid acne / rosacea / perioral dermatitis:** oral, inhaled, topical or illicit bleaching steroids.
**Gram-negative folliculitis:** long-term oral tetracyclines for acne/rosacea → overgrowth of *Klebsiella*, *Enterobacter*, *Proteus*.
**Malassezia folliculitis:** yeast in oily follicles, often after antibiotics or steroids.
**Hot-tub folliculitis:** *Pseudomonas* in under-chlorinated spa water.
**"More antibiotics will fix stubborn 'acne'"**: Gram-negative and Malassezia folliculitis are caused or worsened by antibiotics.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Each mimic has a **different driver** in or around the follicle.

mech.t: Comedone formation, sebum and C. acnes inflammation.
mech.caption: Acne starts with a comedone; mimics usually don't.

mech.t: Neurovascular dysregulation, cathelicidin, Demodex and UV.
mech.caption: Rosacea favours the convex central face.

mech.t: Steroids alter follicular keratinisation and local immunity, giving monomorphic lesions.
mech.caption: Perioral dermatitis spares a rim around the lips.

mech.t: Antibiotics allow Gram-negative bacteria or Malassezia yeast to fill follicles; hot tubs deliver Pseudomonas.

ul: **Rosacea fulminans (pyoderma faciale):** explosive painful papules, pustules and nodules on a red swollen central face in young women; systemically well (unlike acne fulminans).
**Steroid acne:** sudden monomorphic papules/pustules on chest/back; few comedones.
**Perioral dermatitis:** papules around mouth with vermilion sparing; often after facial steroid.
**Gram-negative folliculitis:** new perinasal pustules after months of tetracycline that initially worked.
**Malassezia:** itchy monomorphic follicular pustules on chest/back.
**Hot-tub:** itchy pustules under the swimsuit line 1–4 days after spa use.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. Swab pustules and anterior nares (request Gram-negative culture) when acne worsens on long antibiotics. Consider ANA only if lupus is realistic. Do not diagnose rosacea if comedones dominate — rethink acne.

ul: Comedones dominate → it is **acne**.
Ask about steroids, inhalers and antibiotic duration.
Worse on long antibiotics: swab pustules and **anterior nares**; request Gram-negative culture.
ANA only if **lupus** is realistic.
Spa or hot tub in the last few days?

sections.title: Management

blocks.title: Rosacea in depth
blocks.text: Phenotypes, flushing work-up, ocular rosacea, *Demodex* and steroid-induced rosacea now have their own page: [rosacea](condition:rosacea).

ul: Trigger diary, gentle skincare, daily sunscreen; **avoid topical steroids**.
Persistent erythema: topical brimonidine (warn about rebound).
Mild–moderate papulopustular: **ivermectin 1% cream** first-line, or azelaic acid 15%, or metronidazole 0.75%.
Moderate–severe: topical ivermectin **plus** oral **doxycycline 40 mg MR** (licensed) or other tetracycline; erythromycin if tetracyclines unsuitable.
Ocular: lid hygiene, lubricants ± oral tetracycline; **same-day ophthalmology** for pain, photophobia or reduced vision.
Stop the topical/inhaled facial steroid exposure (taper systemic steroids with the original prescriber — never abruptly).
Warn of a rebound flare. Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid; oral tetracycline 6–8 weeks if needed (erythromycin if under 12).

blocks: Perioral dermatitis now has its own page: [Perioral dermatitis](condition:perioral-dermatitis).

ul: Gram-negative: **stop the tetracycline**; swab; specialist options include isotretinoin or culture-guided antibiotics — refer rather than endless antibiotic switches.
Malassezia: topical or oral antifungal per local practice; stop unnecessary antibiotics/steroids.
Hot-tub: usually self-limiting in days; antibiotics only if severe or immunocompromised.
**Urgent dermatology referral.** Do not keep cycling oral antibiotics. Specialist care often uses a short steroid course then isotretinoin (pregnancy exclusions apply).

blocks.title: Check BNF
blocks.text: Confirm doses, pregnancy advice and interactions before prescribing.

ladder.t: Trigger diary, gentle skincare, daily sunscreen; **avoid topical steroids**. Persistent erythema: brimonidine (warn about rebound).
**Ivermectin 1% cream** first line, or azelaic acid 15%, or metronidazole 0.75%. Moderate–severe: add **doxycycline 40 mg MR** (licensed); erythromycin if tetracyclines unsuitable.

Stop the facial steroid; taper systemic steroids with the prescriber, never abruptly. Warn of rebound. Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid; oral tetracycline 6–8 weeks if needed (erythromycin if under 12).
**Gram-negative**: stop the tetracycline, swab, refer (isotretinoin or culture-guided antibiotics). **Malassezia**: topical or oral antifungal; stop unnecessary antibiotics / steroids.
**Urgent dermatology.** Don’t keep cycling oral antibiotics.

refer.t: Ocular pain, photophobia or reduced vision → **ophthalmology**.
**Rosacea fulminans** or suspected acne fulminans → dermatology.
Acne worse on long tetracyclines: culture for Gram-negatives and **stop the antibiotic**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Ocular pain, photophobia or reduced vision → same-day ophthalmology.
Rosacea fulminans or suspected acne fulminans → urgent dermatology.
Phyma needing procedural treatment; diagnostic doubt.
Acne worsening on long tetracyclines → culture for Gram-negatives; stop the antibiotic.
Scarring (rosacea fulminans), ocular rosacea, prolonged mistreatment.
Good once the right diagnosis is made.

pearls: **No comedones + flushing + central face = rosacea until proven otherwise.**
Maintenance topical therapy is often needed — rosacea is relapsing.
Pharmacists often spot inhaled-steroid perioral dermatitis — advise rinsing/wiping the face after inhalers.
Laser/IPL for telangiectasia is usually private, not NHS-funded.
For the full rosacea ladder by phenotype, see [rosacea](condition:rosacea).

quiz.q: Which single sign separates acne from its mimics?
quiz.a: Comedones: present in acne, absent in rosacea and the folliculitis mimics.

quiz.q: New perinasal pustules after months of a tetracycline that first worked?
quiz.a: Gram-negative folliculitis: swab (incl. nares), stop the tetracycline, refer.

quiz.q: Papules around the mouth with a clear rim at the lip border after a steroid cream?
quiz.a: Perioral (periorificial) dermatitis: stop the steroid, warn of rebound.

quiz.q: Explosive painful facial nodules in a young woman who is systemically well?
Itchy follicular pustules under the swimsuit 2 days after a spa?
